column4: The section names root ر د ي (B003) for falling into a well and exposure to ruin; 5:3 uses its related form for an animal killed by falling, making the physical fall explicit while changing its cause and victim.

The section names root ر د ي (B003) for falling and facing ruin; in 20:16 Moses is warned that following desire away from the Hour will make him perish, turning the fall into the consequence of heedless deviation.
The section's downward direction culminates in a look below; 37:55 has the saved speaker look and see his former companion in Hell, supplying the view that 37:56's near-ruin recalls.
The section names root ر د ي (B003) for ruin by falling; 37:56 uses that root when the speaker says his worldly companion nearly ruined him, and 37:55 places that companion in Hell.
The section contrasts the one who falls with the one kept safe; after 37:56's near-disaster, the speaker credits his Lord's favor for not being among the punished, showing what turned him aside.

The section pictures a man tumbling down and sets descent against an upward turn; 22:31 likens associating partners with God to falling from the sky, snatched by birds or swept far away by wind, giving the downward direction a spiritual meaning.

The section itself contrasts a structure collapsing into Hell with one founded on taqwa and riḍwān, roots it links to the surah's fifth and twenty-first verses; the unstable edge makes the fall an image of a false foundation.
The section's man approaches a well-mouth and falls; 3:103 recalls people at the edge of a fiery pit whom God rescued, reversing the image from an unhelped plunge to deliverance.

The section says wealth cannot help the man when he falls; 28:81 describes Qarun and his home swallowed by the earth, with no company able to help him, making that claim concrete in the case of a rich man.
The section's plunge begins at a well; 12:15 recounts Joseph's brothers deliberately lowering him into a well, while God's inspiration preserves him, a descent with a different outcome from ruin.
The section's well is a downward opening; 12:19 has a water-drawer raise Joseph from a well, reversing the direction and showing that a descent need not be the final end.
The section's wealth cannot arrest a fall; in 18:42 a garden's trellises collapse over its owner and he wrings his hands over what he spent, making material possession fail amid physical collapse.
The section says the falling man's wealth cannot help him; after the garden collapses in 18:42, 18:43 says he has no group to help him against God, completing the helplessness.
The section turns from failed worldly wealth to seeking the Lord's face; after the ruined garden in 18:42, 18:44 locates true protection and the best outcome with God.

The section's unstable mosque falls from its foundation; 16:26 recounts earlier plotters whose building was torn from its foundations and whose roof fell over them, a matching collapse that exposes the plot.
The section develops a heedless approach to a hole; 67:16 warns people who feel secure that the earth may swallow them suddenly, making presumed safety itself part of the danger.
The section sets a downward fate against the God-fearing person's safety; 101:8 makes light scales the condition of a bad destination, linking the abyss that follows in 101:9 to moral measure.
The section's plunge ends in ruin; 101:9 names the light-weighted person's destination as Hawiya, the abyss, giving the downward image an explicit afterlife endpoint.
The section's fall ends in fire; after naming Hawiya in 101:9, 101:11 identifies it as a fiercely heated fire.
The section warns of falling into fire; in 21:68 Abraham's opponents order that he be burned, setting up the reversal in the next ayah.
The section contrasts entering fire with being kept away from it; 21:69 makes the fire cool and safe for Abraham, reversing the fire's destructive action in the preceding verse.
The section contrasts a fall into ruin with protection; after the failed attempt to burn Abraham in 21:68-69, 21:70 says the plotters were made the losers.
The section's fire is a destination of destruction; 37:97 has Abraham's people build a structure and cast him into a blaze, a direct fire scene whose outcome differs in 37:98.
The section's pious person is kept away from fire; after Abraham is cast into it in 37:97, 37:98 says his opponents' scheme failed, completing the reversal.
The section says the most mindful person will be kept away from the Fire; 21:101 likewise says those for whom God's good promise has gone ahead are kept far from it.
The section depicts safety from the Fire; after 21:101 says the promised ones are kept far away, 21:102 adds that they will not hear its faintest sound, describing the distance's result.
The section distinguishes between entering the Fire and being kept away; 19:71 says all come to it, setting the boundary that 19:72 draws.
The section's God-fearing person is kept away from the Fire; after 19:71 says all come to it, 19:72 says God saves the mindful and leaves wrongdoers there on their knees.
The section's most mindful person is kept from the Fire; 44:56 describes the people of the Garden as protected from Hell's punishment, a parallel final safety.
The section's pious person is turned aside from the Fire; 52:18 says the people of the Garden enjoy their provision while their Lord protects them from Hell's punishment.
The section says a man's wealth does not avail him when he falls; in 69:28 the judged speaker says his wealth did not help him, a close formulation in its own reckoning scene.
The section says the falling man's possessions cannot save him; 69:29 adds that his authority has vanished, extending failed wealth to failed status.
The section's fall reveals helplessness; after the speaker's lost wealth and authority in 69:28-29, 69:30 orders him seized, showing the reversal of worldly power.
The section links ruin to fire; after the seizure in 69:30, 69:31 sends the judged person into the Blaze.
The section's steep ascent is freeing a slave and feeding in hunger; 69:34 says the condemned person did not urge feeding the poor, a specific reversal tied to the Fire in the surrounding verses.
The section says wealth cannot help the falling man; after the condemned person's failure to feed the poor in 69:34, 69:35 says he has no devoted friend to help him.
The section says wealth is useless at the moment of ruin; 111:2 says Abu Lahab's wealth and earnings did not benefit him, and 111:3 gives the fiery end.
The section names the Fire as the consequence awaiting the ruined person; after 111:2 denies that wealth helped Abu Lahab, 111:3 places him in a flaming fire.
The section says wealth cannot rescue a person from the fall; 3:10 says disbelievers' wealth and children will not avail them against God and identifies them as fuel for the Fire.
The section connects turning from guidance with the Fire; 70:15 introduces the blazing flame that seizes those described in the following verses.
The section's Fire is a destructive endpoint; 70:16 describes the flame stripping away, sharpening the consequence announced in 70:15.

The section names the root ج ن ب (B003) for being turned aside from something; 70:17 says the flame calls the one who turned his back and turned away, the reverse of the mindful person being kept away from it.
The section contrasts spending wealth to purify oneself with a ruinous descent; 70:18 completes the description of the flame's target as the one who gathered wealth and hoarded it.
The section sets the generous, God-fearing person against the one led to ruin; after the hoarder of 70:18, 70:22 introduces those who persist in prayer as an exception.
The section's upward path includes giving wealth; 70:24 says the people of prayer recognize a due in their wealth, a concrete counterpart to the section's generous path.
The section makes feeding the hungry part of the steep ascent; 70:25 specifies the needy and deprived as recipients of that due.
The section presents a reminder for the one who fears; 70:27 describes the people of the upward path as fearing their Lord's punishment.
The section contrasts the one entering Fire with the one turned away from it; after describing the God-fearing group in 70:22-34, 70:35 places them in honored Gardens.
The section distinguishes the Fire from the person kept away from it; 74:42 asks the condemned what brought them into Saqar, setting up their own account.
The section's ascent is a path of mindful action; 74:43 names failure to pray among the condemned's reasons for entering Saqar.
The section makes feeding the hungry part of the steep path; 74:44 gives failure to feed the poor as a reason for entering Saqar, the direct opposite.
The section contrasts a God-fearing direction with ruin; 74:45 says the condemned joined in vain discourse, another part of their account of how they reached Saqar.
The section's vertical choice ends in either safety or ruin; 74:46 says the people of Saqar denied the Day of Recompense.
The section's falling ends in an irreversible consequence; 74:47 closes the account of Saqar with the certainty that finally came to its occupants.
The section says wealth cannot protect someone who falls; 104:2 depicts a person accumulating and counting wealth, establishing the possession later shown not to preserve him.
The section makes worldly wealth powerless at ruin; 104:3 says the hoarder thinks his wealth will make him last forever, exposing the false security before 104:4's crushing.
The section's fall leads to destruction; after the false security of 104:3, 104:4 says the hoarder will be cast into the Crusher.
The section connects ruin with Fire; 104:6 identifies the Crusher as a fire kindled by God.
The section says no wealth helps at the fall; 13:18 pictures the wrongdoer wishing to ransom himself with everything on earth and its like, but facing an evil reckoning and Hell.
The section says wealth cannot secure the falling person and directs giving toward God's face; 26:88 says wealth and children will not benefit on the Day.
The section opposes empty wealth to sincere orientation toward the Lord's face; 26:89 names a sound heart as the exception to 26:88's failed wealth.

The section names root ع ل و (B001) in الأعلى and its B006 branch for a call to a high place; 87:1 commands glorification of the Lord Most High, locating the upward direction in God rather than a human claimant.
The section says the wretched enter Fire and the mindful are kept away; 87:12 identifies the wretched person's destination as the great Fire.
The section's Fire is a final ruin; 87:13 says its occupant neither dies nor lives, describing the condition after the entry in 87:12.
The section's upward path gives wealth to purify oneself; 87:14 says success belongs to the one who purifies himself, a direct ethical counterpart.
The section directs the face toward the Lord Most High; 87:15 joins remembering the Lord's name with prayer as the purified person's practice.
The section's highest direction opposes the fall toward worldly ruin; 87:16 says people prefer the nearer life, naming the lower preference that opposes the section's turn toward the Lord.
The section turns toward the Lord Most High; 87:17 says the Hereafter is better and more lasting than the nearer life, completing 87:16's contrast.
The section describes an upward alternative to falling; 90:11 calls the unattempted steep path an ascent, giving the vertical image an ethical action.
The section's image turns a vertical route into moral choice; 90:12 asks what the steep path is, which 90:13-16 answers.
The section says the steep ascent is freeing a slave and giving wealth; 90:13 specifies freeing a neck as the first act on that path.
The section names feeding during hunger as part of the upward path; 90:14 introduces feeding on a day of famine.
The section names the ascent's care for the vulnerable; 90:15 specifies an orphan near of kin as a recipient of food.
The section names feeding the hungry as the ascent's work; 90:16 specifies a person in severe need, completing the examples begun in 90:14.
The section's ascent belongs to the mindful; 90:17 adds belief, mutual urging of patience, and mutual urging of compassion as the path's community and moral direction.
The section's upward path gives wealth away and feeds the hungry; 76:8 depicts righteous people giving food to the needy, orphan, and captive despite their own desire for it.
The section says the giving is only to seek the Lord's face, with no favor owed in return; 76:9 makes the feeding likewise free of any wish for reward or thanks.
The section calls this a reminder for the one who fears; 76:10 says the givers fear a severe day from their Lord.
The section contrasts the Fire with the person kept from it; after the fear in 76:10, 76:11 says God protects the givers from that day's evil and gives them radiance and joy.
The section presents giving wealth as the upward path; 2:177 defines righteousness by giving loved wealth to relatives, orphans, needy people, travelers, and freeing captives.
The section says wealth is given solely in seeking the Lord's face; 2:272 connects spending good to the spender and explicitly locates the expenditure in seeking God's face.
The section makes giving wealth part of turning upward; 3:92 says righteousness is not attained until one spends what one loves, specifying the cost of that orientation.
The section describes giving wealth to purify oneself; 9:103 tells the Messenger to take charity from people's wealth to cleanse and purify them, giving that act a direct parallel.
The section directs giving toward the Lord's face; 30:38 names relatives, needy people, and travelers as recipients, then links giving to those who desire God's face and success.
The section says the generous person gives wealth to purify himself; 91:9 says the one who purifies the soul succeeds, a close statement of what that giving seeks.
The section sets the mindful person against ruin; 91:10 gives the contrary outcome to the soul's success, illuminating the section's two directions.
The section links giving wealth and mindful orientation to safety from ruin; 61:10 introduces a trade that saves believers from painful punishment.
The section's upward turn involves giving wealth; 61:11 identifies belief and striving with wealth and selves as the saving trade introduced in 61:10.
The section contrasts the Fire with being turned away from it; 61:12 gives the promised outcome of the saving trade as forgiveness and Gardens.

The section says wealth is spent seeking the Lord's face and a higher outcome; 9:111 depicts God purchasing believers' selves and wealth in return for the Garden, recasting possession as directed toward the final home.
The section says wealth cannot be held back until the fall and directs it toward God; 14:31 urges believers to spend from their provision before the Day when no trade or friendship can help.
The section names root ج ن ب (B003) for keeping someone away; 39:17 describes people who avoid false gods and turn to God, linking deliberate avoidance to good news.
The section names root ج ن ب (B003) for being turned aside; 4:31 uses its avoidance sense for major sins and connects that avoidance to forgiveness and an honorable entrance.
The section's root ج ن ب (B003) describes keeping away; 53:32 applies it to avoiding major sins and indecencies, a specific form of the mindful separation in the section.
The section portrays a companion nearly pulling someone into ruin; 25:27 shows a wrongdoer biting his hand in remorse when consequences arrive, with the cause explained in the next two ayat.
The section's falling man can be led toward destruction by another; 25:28 names the wrongdoer's regret at having taken a certain person as a friend.
The section says a companion can nearly bring someone to ruin; 25:29 says that friend turned him away from the Reminder after it came, specifying the lure's effect.

The section's worldly companion nearly pulls the speaker toward Hell; 6:71 depicts someone lured away by devils and confused while companions call him back to God's guidance, making the choice of direction explicit.
The section describes a companion whose influence ends at Hell; 2:166 shows leaders disowning their followers when they see punishment and their ties breaking.
The section's falling person cannot be saved by what he has; 2:167 shows the followers wishing to return so they could disown their leaders, extending the failed-companionship scene.
The section's deceiving companion leads toward ruin; 14:21 stages followers and arrogant leaders before God, where the leaders cannot offer the rescue their followers seek.
The section's companion can pull someone toward destruction; 14:22 has Satan disown those who followed his invitation, specifying the betrayal after the lure.
The section describes a fall caused by heedless turning; 43:36 says one who turns away from the Reminder is assigned a devil as companion, joining the turn with a destructive guide.
The section's companion pulls the unwary toward ruin; 43:37 says such companions divert people from the path while they think they are guided.
The section's near-fall is tied to a worldly companion; 43:38 has the deluded person wish for a great distance from that companion when both arrive before God.
The section's worldly friend nearly brings his companion to Hell; 43:67 reverses that relation by saying close friends become enemies on that Day except the mindful.
The section presents Pharaoh's claim to be highest as a public false elevation; 79:23 shows him gathering and calling his people, the public setting for the claim in 79:24.
The section names root ع ل و (B001) through الأعلى and points to Pharaoh's false claim; 79:24 has Pharaoh call himself the most high lord, a direct counterfeit of the section's Lord Most High.
The section says the one who claims the highest position is brought down; after Pharaoh's claim in 79:24, 79:25 says God seized him as punishment.
The section invokes a reminder for the one who fears; after Pharaoh is seized, 79:26 calls the event a lesson for whoever fears, completing the warning.

The section's upward direction is a summons toward the Lord Most High; 40:36 has Pharaoh order a tower built so he can try to reach heaven and inspect Moses' God, an attempted ascent that confuses height with authority.
The section distinguishes true elevation from a false claim; 40:37 says Pharaoh's tower plan only led to loss and that he was turned from the way.
The section contrasts the Lord Most High with a human claim to supremacy; 43:51 has Pharaoh boast of Egypt and the rivers flowing beneath him, grounding his claim in worldly height and power.
The section's false claimant draws others toward ruin; 43:54 says Pharaoh made his people disregard the truth and they obeyed him, showing the reach of his authority.
The section says false elevation ends in being brought down; after Pharaoh's boast and his people's obedience, 43:55 says God took retribution on them.
The section turns from false height to a fall; 43:56 says Pharaoh and his people were drowned and made an example for later generations.
The section exposes a false claim to the highest lordship; 28:38 has Pharaoh claim divinity and ask for a tower from which to look toward Moses' God, pairing the claim with an attempted ascent.
The section's false high claimant is brought down; after Pharaoh's tower claim in 28:38, 28:40 says he and his army were seized and cast into the sea.
The section says orientation ends either upward or in ruin; 28:41 depicts Pharaoh's leaders as calling to the Fire and lacking help on the Day.
The section contrasts the downward fall with the upward face turned to God; 7:12 has Iblis claim superiority over Adam, showing a creature's false self-elevation.
The section's false height ends below; after Iblis's boast in 7:12, 7:13 commands him to descend because of his arrogance.
The section contrasts true highness with a creature's pride; 38:75 rebukes Iblis for refusing to bow before Adam.
The section's vertical axis separates God's true height from self-asserted rank; 38:76 repeats Iblis's claim that he is better because he was made of fire while Adam was made of clay.
The section depicts a false elevation ending in a fall; after Iblis's superiority claim in 38:76, 38:77 commands him to leave.
The section turns from false highness to ruin; 38:78 places a curse on Iblis until the Day of Judgment after his rejection.
The section juxtaposes a fall below with the Lord Most High; 17:37 sets a boundary on human height, saying a person cannot split the earth or reach the mountains in height.
The section exposes Pharaoh's false claim to highness; 28:83 says the Hereafter belongs to those who do not seek exaltation or corruption on earth.
The section turns the reader upward toward the Lord Most High; 35:10 says good speech ascends to Him and righteous action raises it, making moral action a literal upward motion.

The section presents highness as the direction of guidance; 6:125 uses climbing into the sky as an image of the constriction of misguidance, a useful limit showing that upward motion in the section is moral orientation rather than literal altitude.
The section contrasts the low fall with the Lord Most High; 58:11 says God raises believers and those given knowledge by degrees, a direct moral use of elevation.
The section's image gives two opposed directions; 2:257 describes God bringing believers from darkness to light while false allies bring others from light into darkness, ending in the Fire.
The section's good direction seeks the Lord's pleasure and avoids ruin; 5:16 says those who follow God's pleasure are guided to paths of peace and brought from darkness to light.
